documents: Stott et al., Machine learning and marsquakes: a tool to predict atmospheric-seismic noise for the NASA InSight mission (PDF, 49 pages; the PDF header marks it as the preprint submitted to Geophys. J. Int.)
pages_convention: PDF pages counted from 1 (these coincide with the page numbers printed on the manuscript)

entry.evidence: This demonstrates that atmospheric injection inhibits the discrimination of data of a seismic origin.

sequences.source_document: Stott et al. GJI paper (PDF as supplied)

steps.action: Report from the MQS catalogue that marsquake detections nearly vanish in the turbulent northern-winter period and cluster in calm evening hours.
steps.quote: However, between sols 500 and 800 only 27 of these 951 events were observed.

steps.action: Pose the problem of separating seismometer data into atmospherically induced and seismic components.
steps.quote: the separation of the seismometer data into atmospherically induced and seismic origin components is of interest

steps.action: Take the expected wind, pressure and temperature noise injection from the pre-landing noise model and later in situ studies. This includes the drag/lift forcing in Eq. 1.
steps.quote: The impact of wind, pressure and temperature on the seismic data was predicted in the pre-landing noise model of Mimoun et al. (2017).

steps.action: Design the study as supervised regression from eight atmospheric inputs to three-axis seismic energy envelopes. Two event-class bandwidths are chosen: 0.4-1 Hz and the 2.2-2.6 Hz mode.
steps.quote: we formulate a supervised learning regression style problem, to predict the seismic energy from the atmospheric data

steps.action: Build the preprocessing pipeline. It covers response removal, rotation, band filtering, 10 s envelopes, resampling to 1 sps, deglitching, peak removal, masks, log transform and normalisation, yielding about 30 million samples.
steps.quote: The preprocessing must blend together this data taken at different sampling rates

steps.action: Display the input-output scatter matrices for three seasons. These show the atmospheric-seismic relation changing diurnally and seasonally, interpreted with turbulence regimes from Chatain et al.
steps.quote: It can be seen that the relationship between the seismic data and each of these variables changes over both the Martian sol and season

steps.action: Implement global and local Gaussian process regression models and a multilayer perceptron. The GP kernel is selected on test RMSE (Table 1) and the NN architecture by a layer and neuron sweep (Figure 3).
steps.quote: Four models with different kernels were trained on the LF data to identify the best choice.

steps.action: Check the NN for overfitting by comparing training and held-out test loss over 100 epochs.
steps.quote: The test loss is fluctuating around the training loss but follows its trend, indicating there is no overfitting.

steps.action: Compare the three models' held-out RMSE for LF and HF bands overall (Table 2) and on three exemplar sols (Table 3).
steps.quote: The neural network approach provides the lowest error, followed by the local and then global GP models.

steps.action: Examine residuals and their distributions across three seasons and turbulence regimes to check that prediction quality is stable. Transient-level and daytime failures are noted.
steps.quote: indicating there is no major change in the prediction quality over the seasons

steps.action: From the models' failure to predict ambient 2.4 Hz variation in quiet periods, suggest that the ambient modulation of the 2.4 Hz mode is not of local atmospheric origin.
steps.quote: fail to predict the overall ambient variation of the 2.4Hz suggests that it not not generated with local atmospheric effects

steps.action: Use the NN noise prediction to compute the log-residual SNR for every catalogued event in both bands (Appendix C). Example events are analysed in Figures 11-12, including phase structure and gust contamination.
steps.quote: This SNR has been calculated for every event (with available data) in the catalogue

steps.action: Establish from the catalogue-wide SNR (Figure 13) that separable low-frequency energy recurs in HF, VF and 2.4 Hz events.
steps.quote: is not unique to that event and is a consistent feature which occurs regularly for all types of high frequency event

steps.action: Exclude an observational distance bias by plotting SNR against catalogue distance and magnitude (Figure 14). They find no distance dependence but a magnitude correlation.
steps.quote: There is no clear dependence on distance for the presence of low frequency energy and so the observation is not because these events are close

steps.action: Retain the interpretation that marsquake frequency classes form a continuum rather than disparate groups.
steps.quote: both the high and low frequency event classes are not disparate groupings and that they instead follow a continuum in frequency content

steps.action: Build a detection algorithm with a variable threshold. The residual is detrended with moving medians, thresholded at mean plus 3 SD over 2 h windows, and outliers are required on all three components with positive amplitude.
steps.quote: We propose the following algorithm to calculate a variable threshold

steps.action: Test detection against the MQS catalogue: 25 of 32 LF/BB and 314 of 377 HF events are recovered. The misses are explained by glitches, contamination, low quality and energy below 0.4 Hz.
steps.quote: The detection algorithm performed on the LF, 0.4-1Hz, band found 25 of 32 low frequency and broadband quakes

steps.action: Filter the new detections (duration at least 2 min, SNR above 1.2) and review them manually. This yields 9 LF and 25 HF new marsquakes (32 unique) plus 34 possible ones (Tables 4, 5, A2, A3).
steps.quote: From this group, we propose 9 new marsquakes which are presented in Table 4.

steps.action: Check one new LF event (sol 452) against the confidence interval of the independently trained local GP model (Figure 16).
steps.quote: it is clearly separate from the environment and also exceeds the confidence interval of the local GP model

steps.action: Estimate empirical detectivity by comparing the cumulative distribution of the detection threshold over the mission with the levels reached by detected events (Figure 18).
steps.quote: Tracking this threshold over the mission enables an estimate the detectability of a marsquake similar to one in the catalogue over the mission.

steps.action: Conclude that the NN noise predictor is a usable tool for event analysis, detection of new marsquakes and detectivity estimation.
steps.quote: This has led to the detection of 32 new marsquakes and a further 34 possible candidates.

end.claim: Neural-network and GP regressions predict the atmospheric seismic noise in the 0.4-1 Hz and 2.2-2.6 Hz bands with held-out RMSE of about 0.067 (NN). The resulting SNR enables event analysis, detection of 32 new marsquakes plus 34 candidates, and empirical detectivity estimates.

decisive_move.sentence: Without the regression model that predicts seismic energy from atmospheric data (step 7), there would be no residual SNR, no detections and no detectivity estimate.

gates.evidence: The data are archival mission data acquired without any hypothesis of the paper. The tool faced tests it could fail: held-out RMSE (p.13, 15) and recovery of MQS catalogue events (p.26). The continuum claim faced only a distance check (p.23). Detection thresholds (3 SD, SNR>1.2, 2 min) and model choices are not stated as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Gaussian process regression (Williams & Rasmussen 2006) via the GPy library
Multilayer perceptron neural network in Keras with ReLU and the ADAM optimiser

novelty_claims.quote: This algorithm finds 32 previously undetected marsquakes, with another 34 possible candidates.
we propose 9 new marsquakes which are presented in Table 4
The manual review of these detections gives an extra 25 new marsquakes presented in Table 5

limits: The supplied PDF carries a preprint header ("has not yet been peer reviewed") although it was supplied as the published paper. No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded. Sub-claims at other statuses: the frequency-content continuum is best_explanation (only a distance-bias rival is checked). The 32 new marsquakes rest on unspecified manual review and are not confirmed independently. Detectivity is estimate_with_resolution in form, but no uncertainty is given and the authors call it only empirical. The non-atmospheric origin of the ambient 2.4 Hz modulation is a suggestion only. No false-detection rate is quantified, although sources of false detections are listed (p.27). No sensitivity to the detection thresholds (3 SD, 2 h window, SNR 1.2, 2 min) is reported. RMSE values carry no uncertainty, and some local-GP sols were removed from the error calculation (p.16). Inference: the held-out test set is a random 20% of 1-sps samples, so test samples are temporally adjacent to training samples, and the held-out check may overstate skill. The composition is coded capability_first loosely: the paper opens with a stated problem rather than a capability, and the capability then generates the LF-energy observation.
